variants.name: Health Insurance
variants.description: Questions against the bundled synthetic Health Insurance sample (members, plans, providers and claims of 2024 and 2025, money in cents), each guarding a planted trap. Select its PostgreSQL datasource with a saved dataset containing the health_insurance tables and views; Settings, Testing Data loads both.

cases.question: Which specialties are we paying the highest share of what they bill?
cases.intent: Divide paid by billed — two genuinely different money columns — instead of dividing one amount column by itself.
cases.notes:
billed_amount_cents, allowed_amount_cents and paid_amount_cents all read like "the amount", so billed/billed or allowed/allowed is one keystroke away and returns 1.0000 for every specialty, turning the ranking into alphabetical noise. Paid over billed across the 1164 non-test claims — the reference obeys the dataset's default filter and drops is_test claims — gives Family Medicine 0.4847, Dermatology 0.4309, Oncology 0.3843, Cardiology 0.3216, Behavioral Health 0.2840, Radiology 0.2442, Orthopedics 0.1895, Emergency Medicine 0.1409 — the smallest gap between adjacent specialties is 0.038, so the ordering is not a rounding artefact. The shares are checked by the result set; the text check only asks for the top specialty by name. Guards against the degenerate-ratio regression where the engine picks two names for the same column. Trap (validated 2026-09-23): the trapSql divides billed by billed and returns 1.0000 for all eight specialties. Accepts a fraction or a percentage — the question names no unit; alternative verified 2026-09-23: ROUND(100.0 * paid / billed, 2) returns the same 8 specialties in the same order, Family Medicine 48.47 down to Emergency Medicine 14.09, each exactly the reference × 100.

Trap query (must return different rows): SELECT provider.specialty, ROUND(CAST(SUM(claim.billed_amount_cents) AS DECIMAL(38,6)) / SUM(claim.billed_amount_cents), 4) AS paid_share_of_billed FROM health_insurance.claims claim JOIN health_insurance.providers provider ON provider.id = claim.provider_id WHERE claim.is_test = false GROUP BY provider.specialty

Alternative reference the branch also accepted: SELECT provider.specialty, ROUND(100.0 * SUM(claim.paid_amount_cents) / SUM(claim.billed_amount_cents), 2) AS paid_share_of_billed_pct FROM health_insurance.claims claim JOIN health_insurance.providers provider ON provider.id = claim.provider_id WHERE claim.is_test = false GROUP BY provider.specialty ORDER BY paid_share_of_billed_pct DESC, provider.specialty

Paraphrases: Which specialties get paid the largest portion of the amount they bill us? | Rank the specialties by how much of their billed charges we actually pay.

Moved from feat/engine-eval-loop (branch category ratio-trap, provenance hand).

expectedSql.postgres: SELECT provider.specialty, ROUND(SUM(claim.paid_amount_cents)::numeric / SUM(claim.billed_amount_cents), 4) AS paid_share_of_billed FROM health_insurance.claims claim JOIN health_insurance.providers provider ON provider.id = claim.provider_id WHERE claim.is_test = false GROUP BY provider.specialty ORDER BY paid_share_of_billed DESC, provider.specialty

cases.question: On the claims we paid, what share of the allowed amount did the plan cover rather than the member, by plan tier?
cases.intent: The second ratio pair: paid over ALLOWED, not paid over billed and not allowed over allowed.
cases.notes:
On the 785 non-test PAID claims allowed = paid + member_responsibility, so paid/allowed is the plan's share and it tracks the tier's coinsurance: PLATINUM 0.8664, GOLD 0.8500, SILVER 0.8039, BRONZE 0.7392 — the reference obeys the dataset's default filter and drops is_test claims. Two wrong denominators are equally available: allowed/allowed gives a flat 1.0000, and billed instead of allowed gives GOLD 0.4317, BRONZE 0.3826, SILVER 0.3715, PLATINUM 0.3646 — which inverts the ranking and would report BRONZE members as better covered than PLATINUM ones. The shares are checked by the result set; the text check only asks for the top tier by name. Guards against an answer that is plausible, ordered and wrong because the denominator came from the wrong column. Trap (validated 2026-09-23): the trapSql uses billed instead of allowed as the denominator and returns GOLD 0.4317, BRONZE 0.3826, SILVER 0.3715, PLATINUM 0.3646 — the inverted ranking described above. Accepts a fraction or a percentage — the question names no unit; alternative verified 2026-09-23: ROUND(100.0 * paid / allowed, 2) returns the same 4 tiers, PLATINUM 86.64, GOLD 85.00, SILVER 80.39, BRONZE 73.92, each exactly the reference × 100.

Trap query (must return different rows): SELECT plan.tier, ROUND(CAST(SUM(claim.paid_amount_cents) AS DECIMAL(38,6)) / SUM(claim.billed_amount_cents), 4) AS plan_share FROM health_insurance.claims claim JOIN health_insurance.plans plan ON plan.id = claim.plan_id WHERE claim.status = 'PAID' AND claim.is_test = false GROUP BY plan.tier

Alternative reference the branch also accepted: SELECT plan.tier, ROUND(100.0 * SUM(claim.paid_amount_cents) / SUM(claim.allowed_amount_cents), 2) AS plan_share_of_allowed_pct FROM health_insurance.claims claim JOIN health_insurance.plans plan ON plan.id = claim.plan_id WHERE claim.status = 'PAID' AND claim.is_test = false GROUP BY plan.tier ORDER BY plan_share_of_allowed_pct DESC, plan.tier

Paraphrases: By plan tier, how much of the allowed amount on paid claims did the plan pick up versus the member? | For paid claims, what portion of the allowed amount was covered by the plan in each tier?

Moved from feat/engine-eval-loop (branch category ratio-trap, provenance hand).

expectedSql.postgres: SELECT plan.tier, ROUND(SUM(claim.paid_amount_cents)::numeric / SUM(claim.allowed_amount_cents), 4) AS plan_share_of_allowed FROM health_insurance.claims claim JOIN health_insurance.plans plan ON plan.id = claim.plan_id WHERE claim.status = 'PAID' AND claim.is_test = false GROUP BY plan.tier ORDER BY plan_share_of_allowed DESC, plan.tier

cases.question: How do our claims break down by currency?
cases.intent: Group by a column that holds exactly one value — the answer has to say so instead of presenting 100% as a finding.
cases.notes:
currency is 'USD' on all 1200 claims and a CHECK constraint allows nothing else; the reference obeys the dataset's default filter, so its single row covers the 1164 non-test claims. The breakdown is one row either way, and the useful answer states that every claim is in a single currency rather than dressing a constant up as a distribution or implying an FX comparison the data cannot support. Guards against reporting a one-row group-by as if it were a comparison. Trap (validated 2026-09-23): the trapSql infers the currency from the member's country — the rubric's named failure of inventing CAD for Canadian members — and returns USD 1044, CAD 120 against the reference's single USD 1164 row. Grouping by the constant column cannot be the trap here, because it is the reference; the rubric carries that half of the case.

Trap query (must return different rows): SELECT CASE WHEN country.name = 'Canada' THEN 'CAD' ELSE claim.currency END AS currency, COUNT(*) AS claims FROM health_insurance.claims claim JOIN health_insurance.members member ON member.id = claim.member_id JOIN health_insurance.regions region ON region.id = member.region_id JOIN health_insurance.states state ON state.id = region.state_id JOIN health_insurance.countries country ON country.code = state.country_code WHERE claim.is_test = false GROUP BY CASE WHEN country.name = 'Canada' THEN 'CAD' ELSE claim.currency END

Paraphrases: What currencies are our claims in, and how many claims are in each? | Show me the split of our claims by currency.

Moved from feat/engine-eval-loop (branch category constant-column, provenance hand).

expectedSql.postgres: SELECT claim.currency, COUNT(*) AS claims FROM health_insurance.claims claim WHERE claim.is_test = false GROUP BY claim.currency ORDER BY claim.currency

cases.judgeRubric: The fixture stores only one currency: every claim is USD, 1164 of them once the dataset's default filter excludes test claims. The correct answer says that all claims are in USD, so there is no currency breakdown to compare. Score pass=true only if the final answer states that every claim is in a single currency (USD) and therefore that there is no breakdown to compare — reporting the count (1164, or 1200 if test claims were kept) or "100%" is fine as long as the answer says the column is constant. Score pass=false if it presents the single value as a meaningful distribution, invents a second currency (e.g. CAD, even though some members are Canadian), or implies a currency comparison the data cannot support. Close but wrong: an answer that shows the one-row table "USD: 1164 claims (100%)" as a breakdown, or comments on the currency mix or suggests comparing currencies, without ever saying the column holds a single value — that must FAIL.

cases.question: How many claims had a prior authorization on file?
cases.intent: Count the populated rows of a mostly-null column instead of grouping by it.
cases.notes:
preauth_code is non-null on only 57 of the 1164 non-test claims the dataset's default filter keeps (95.10% null) and every populated value is distinct (format PA-<year>-<6 digits>), so grouping by preauth_code returns 58 near-useless groups with 1107 claims hidden under a blank key. The answer must be the count of claims that HAVE an authorization — checked by the result set, not by a text match on 57. Guards against the engine presenting the null group as a finding, or reading the blank key as "no authorization required". Trap (validated 2026-09-23): the trapSql groups by preauth_code and returns 58 rows — 57 single-claim codes plus a 1107-claim null bucket — against the reference's single count of 57.

Trap query (must return different rows): SELECT claim.preauth_code, COUNT(*) AS claims FROM health_insurance.claims claim WHERE claim.is_test = false GROUP BY claim.preauth_code

Paraphrases: How many of our claims came with a prior authorization? | What's the number of claims that were prior-authorized?

Moved from feat/engine-eval-loop (branch category empty-column, provenance hand).

expectedSql.postgres: SELECT COUNT(*) AS claims_with_preauth FROM health_insurance.claims claim WHERE claim.preauth_code IS NOT NULL AND claim.is_test = false

cases.question: Which specialties submitted exactly 48 claims?
cases.intent: A HAVING-style question whose answer is a tie, so no arbitrary tie-break can hide.
cases.notes:
Oncology and Emergency Medicine each submitted exactly 48 claims; the next smallest specialty is Radiology at 133, so the tie is isolated and it holds whether or not test claims are excluded (both are 48 either way) — the reference still obeys the dataset's default filter rather than modelling the looser form. A "which specialty submitted the fewest claims" phrasing would let a LIMIT 1 silently drop one of the tied specialties, so the question asks for the tie explicitly and both names must appear. Guards against answers that report one arbitrary winner from a tied group. Trap (validated 2026-09-23): the trapSql takes the lowest-volume specialty with LIMIT 1 and returns Emergency Medicine alone (48). The default filter cannot serve as this case's trap: the tie holds with test claims included.

Trap query (must return different rows): SELECT provider.specialty, COUNT(*) AS claims FROM health_insurance.claims claim JOIN health_insurance.providers provider ON provider.id = claim.provider_id WHERE claim.is_test = false GROUP BY provider.specialty ORDER BY claims, provider.specialty LIMIT 1

Paraphrases: Which specialties have exactly 48 claims on file? | List the specialties that sent us exactly 48 claims.

Moved from feat/engine-eval-loop (branch category ties, provenance hand).

expectedSql.postgres: SELECT provider.specialty, COUNT(*) AS claims FROM health_insurance.claims claim JOIN health_insurance.providers provider ON provider.id = claim.provider_id WHERE claim.is_test = false GROUP BY provider.specialty HAVING COUNT(*) = 48 ORDER BY provider.specialty

cases.question: How many claims were approved in 2024?
cases.intent: Map an adjudicator's word onto the enum the status column actually stores.
cases.notes:
There is no 'APPROVED' status. Across the 1164 non-test claims the dataset's default filter keeps, status is PAID (785), DENIED (206), PENDING (125) or REVERSED (48); in 2024 alone it is PAID 395, DENIED 104, PENDING 70, REVERSED 23. Filtering on the literal word returns 0 rows, and counting every 2024 claim returns 592. The reference obeys the default filter and counts claims whose final status is PAID (395) — REVERSED claims were approved and then unwound, which the answer may mention but must not silently fold in. The count is checked by the result set; the text check asks the answer to name the status it mapped "approved" to, case-insensitively (the old case-sensitive PAID failed "paid claims"). Guards against both the empty-filter failure and a status vocabulary invented from the question's wording. Trap (validated 2026-09-23): the trapSql filters on the question's own word, status = 'APPROVED', and returns 0 against the reference's 395.

Trap query (must return different rows): SELECT COUNT(*) AS approved_claims FROM health_insurance.claims claim WHERE claim.status = 'APPROVED' AND claim.is_test = false AND claim.service_date >= DATE '2024-01-01' AND claim.service_date < DATE '2025-01-01'

Paraphrases: How many claims did we approve in 2024? | What was the count of approved claims for 2024?

Moved from feat/engine-eval-loop (branch category value-vocabulary, provenance hand).

expectedSql.postgres: SELECT COUNT(*) AS approved_claims FROM health_insurance.claims claim WHERE claim.status = 'PAID' AND claim.is_test = false AND claim.service_date >= DATE '2024-01-01' AND claim.service_date < DATE '2025-01-01'

cases.question: What did we pay out in claims in 2019?
cases.intent: The fixture covers 2024 and 2025 only — the agent must say so instead of returning a confident zero or inventing a figure.
cases.notes:
service_date runs 2024-01-01 to 2025-12-31 (619 claims in 2024, 581 in 2025; 592 and 572 once the dataset's default filter drops test claims) and a CHECK constraint forbids anything else, so a 2019 query returns an empty aggregate, not a small one. A bare '$0.00' is technically true, reads like a finding and is the failure this case exists to catch; the honest answer names the covered window. Member dates of birth (1948-2005) are the only earlier dates in the schema and must not be mistaken for claim history. noToolErrors was retired (no reference SQL, and a coverage probe that errors is not a wrong answer); didNotCall create_visual stays as the one tool check — charting a year with no data is always wrong. Guards against silently answering outside the fixture's coverage.

Moved from feat/engine-eval-loop (branch category out-of-scope, provenance hand).
cases.judgeRubric: The question asks about 2019, a year this dataset does not cover: every claim has a service date between 2024-01-01 and 2025-12-31. The correct answer says there is no 2019 claim data and that the data covers 2024 and 2025. Score pass=true only if the final answer makes clear there is no 2019 claim data AND explicitly states the period the data DOES cover (2024 and/or 2025), without inventing any 2019 payout, claim count or trend. Score pass=false if it reports a 2019 figure as if it were a real measurement, presents a bare '0' or '$0' with no statement of what the data covers, or fabricates any claim about 2019 activity. Close but wrong: an answer that says "$0 was paid in 2019" with only a vague caveat ("the data may be incomplete") and no covered years, or one that states the coverage correctly but then presents a 2024 or 2025 total as the answer to the 2019 question — that must FAIL.

cases.question: Who is our most expensive member?
cases.intent: "Expensive" is undefined on this schema — billed, paid and member responsibility name three different members, so the agent must ask.
cases.notes:
Three defensible answers sit in the data: Naomi Sedgewick bills the most (13,426,400 cents), Graham Thistlewood costs the plan the most in payments (3,375,050) and Camille Fontaine carries the most member responsibility (924,034). Whichever the agent picks unasked looks authoritative and is unfalsifiable to the reader, so the pass condition is that it asks which cost measure is meant. No noToolErrors: a clarification has no reference SQL. Guards against confident single-metric guesses on an under-specified money question.

Moved from feat/engine-eval-loop (branch category clarification, provenance hand).
cases.judgeRubric: The question ("Who is our most expensive member?") is ambiguous: "expensive" could mean the amount billed by providers, the amount the plan allowed, the amount the plan actually paid, or the amount the member owed — and these pick different members in this data (Naomi Sedgewick by billed amount, Graham Thistlewood by paid amount, Camille Fontaine by member responsibility). The correct answer is a clarifying question such as "Most expensive by amount billed, by what the plan paid, or by what the member owed?". Score pass=true only if the final answer is itself a clarifying question that offers 2-4 concrete, well-formed options grounded in this claims dataset (naming real notions such as billed amount, allowed amount, paid amount, member responsibility or claim count), and that does not name a member or state any figure as if it were the answer. Score pass=false if it picks a member, invents a cost measure the data does not hold (e.g. premiums paid by the plan), or asks a vague open-ended question with no concrete options. Close but wrong: an answer that names a member for one measure (e.g. "Naomi Sedgewick, by billed amount") and only then offers the other measures as follow-ups, or that asks for clarification but offers a single option — that must FAIL.

cases.question: Which member filed the most claims, and how many?
cases.intent: claims carries member_id only — the answer has to join through to full_name instead of handing back a surrogate key.
cases.notes:
The path is claims.member_id -> members.full_name. Naomi Sedgewick filed 42 claims, ahead of Graham Thistlewood on 38, so the maximum is unique and LIMIT 1 with a name tie-break is deterministic; the reference obeys the dataset's default filter, which happens to move neither figure because neither member has a test claim. Grouping on member_id alone answers the question numerically ("member 7") and is useless to a claims analyst, and member_number (M-1000NN) is only marginally better. The count is checked by the result set; the text check asks for the name. Guards against answers that hand the reader opaque keys instead of member names. Trap (validated 2026-09-23): the trapSql groups on claims.member_id and returns 23, 42 — Naomi Sedgewick's surrogate key instead of her name.

Trap query (must return different rows): SELECT claim.member_id, COUNT(*) AS claims FROM health_insurance.claims claim WHERE claim.is_test = false GROUP BY claim.member_id ORDER BY claims DESC LIMIT 1

Paraphrases: Who has the most claims of any member, and how many do they have? | Which member submitted the largest number of claims, and what is the count?

Moved from feat/engine-eval-loop (branch category id-vs-name, provenance hand).

expectedSql.postgres: SELECT member.full_name AS member, COUNT(*) AS claims FROM health_insurance.claims claim JOIN health_insurance.members member ON member.id = claim.member_id WHERE claim.is_test = false GROUP BY member.full_name ORDER BY claims DESC, member.full_name LIMIT 1

cases.question: What was our net paid by region in 2024?
cases.intent: Net paid is a defined metric — gross payments minus reversals — not a plain SUM of paid_amount_cents.
cases.notes:
The 48 non-test REVERSED claims carry a POSITIVE paid_amount_cents (5,339 to 1,201,981 cents), so summing the column adds money back that was clawed out. Net paid by region in 2024, with the dataset's default filter excluding test claims, is Gulf Coast Texas 6,318,595, Southern California 5,998,841, North Texas 4,087,904, Hudson Valley 3,560,707, Ohio Valley 3,162,873, Northern California 3,133,870, Lower Mainland 1,897,657, Greater Toronto 966,560 cents; the gross figure differs in all eight regions and re-orders them (gross puts Hudson Valley 3rd at 6,374,595 and Ohio Valley 4th, net drops them to 4th and 5th). Region comes from the MEMBER's region_id, not the provider's. The figures are checked by the result set (the old text pattern on 6,318,595 would fail a correct "$63.2K"); the text check asks for the top region by name. Guards against the named metric quietly degrading into SUM(paid_amount_cents). Trap (validated 2026-09-23): the trapSql sums paid_amount_cents gross and returns Gulf Coast Texas 6,852,115, Southern California 6,768,269, Hudson Valley 6,374,595, Ohio Valley 4,566,033, North Texas 4,255,354, Northern California 3,747,132, Lower Mainland 2,022,115 and Greater Toronto 995,854 cents. Accepts cents or dollars — the question names no unit; alternative verified 2026-09-23: the same net sum / 100.0 returns the same 8 regions in the same order, Gulf Coast Texas 63,185.95 down to Greater Toronto 9,665.60 dollars, each exactly the reference ÷ 100.

Trap query (must return different rows): SELECT region.name AS region, SUM(claim.paid_amount_cents) AS paid_cents FROM health_insurance.claims claim JOIN health_insurance.members member ON member.id = claim.member_id JOIN health_insurance.regions region ON region.id = member.region_id WHERE claim.is_test = false AND claim.service_date >= DATE '2024-01-01' AND claim.service_date < DATE '2025-01-01' GROUP BY region.name

Alternative reference the branch also accepted: SELECT region.name AS region, SUM(CASE WHEN claim.status = 'REVERSED' THEN -claim.paid_amount_cents ELSE claim.paid_amount_cents END) / 100.0 AS net_paid_dollars FROM health_insurance.claims claim JOIN health_insurance.members member ON member.id = claim.member_id JOIN health_insurance.regions region ON region.id = member.region_id WHERE claim.is_test = false AND claim.service_date >= DATE '2024-01-01' AND claim.service_date < DATE '2025-01-01' GROUP BY region.name ORDER BY net_paid_dollars DESC, region.name

Paraphrases: Break down 2024 net paid by region. | For 2024, how much net paid did each region account for?

Moved from feat/engine-eval-loop (branch category metric-definition, provenance hand).

expectedSql.postgres: SELECT region.name AS region, SUM(CASE WHEN claim.status = 'REVERSED' THEN -claim.paid_amount_cents ELSE claim.paid_amount_cents END) AS net_paid_cents FROM health_insurance.claims claim JOIN health_insurance.members member ON member.id = claim.member_id JOIN health_insurance.regions region ON region.id = member.region_id WHERE claim.is_test = false AND claim.service_date >= DATE '2024-01-01' AND claim.service_date < DATE '2025-01-01' GROUP BY region.name ORDER BY net_paid_cents DESC, region.name

cases.question: How much did we actually pay out in 2024 once reversals are taken off?
cases.intent: A reversed claim is money returned, not money spent — the sign of paid_amount_cents on REVERSED rows is the whole question.
cases.notes:
The second half of the net-paid trap, stated as a single number so the sign error cannot hide inside a breakdown. In 2024, with the dataset's default filter excluding test claims, gross paid is 35,581,467 cents and the 23 reversed claims carry 3,227,230 cents of it, so net paid is 29,127,007 cents ($291,270.07): summing the column outright overstates the year by 6,454,460 cents, twice the reversed amount, because those payments are both added and never subtracted. The figure is checked by the result set; the numeric half of the old merged pattern was retired, leaving the "revers" word check that asks the answer to say it took reversals off. Guards against an answer that treats REVERSED as merely another status to group by rather than as a negative payment. Recategorised from domain-semantics to metric-definition (2026-09-23): nothing in the data links a REVERSED claim to the PAID claim it reverses, so "subtract reversals" versus "exclude reversed claims" (32,354,237 cents) is a definition, not a fact. The governed `net_paid` metric states the subtracting definition, which this reference follows; in the `bare` arm (no Metrics) the case is expected to fail or to state which definition it used. Trap (validated 2026-09-23): the trapSql sums paid_amount_cents gross and returns 35,581,467 cents against the reference's 29,127,007. Accepts cents or dollars — the question names no unit; alternative verified 2026-09-23: the same net sum / 100.0 returns 291,270.07 dollars, exactly the reference's 29,127,007 ÷ 100.

Trap query (must return different rows): SELECT SUM(claim.paid_amount_cents) AS paid_cents FROM health_insurance.claims claim WHERE claim.is_test = false AND claim.service_date >= DATE '2024-01-01' AND claim.service_date < DATE '2025-01-01'

Alternative reference the branch also accepted: SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN claim.status = 'REVERSED' THEN -claim.paid_amount_cents ELSE claim.paid_amount_cents END) / 100.0 AS net_paid_dollars FROM health_insurance.claims claim WHERE claim.is_test = false AND claim.service_date >= DATE '2024-01-01' AND claim.service_date < DATE '2025-01-01'

Paraphrases: What did we really pay out in 2024 after subtracting reversals? | Net of reversals, how much did we pay in 2024?

Moved from feat/engine-eval-loop (branch category metric-definition, provenance hand).

cases.question: How many claims do we have for March 2024 dates of service?
cases.intent: Synthetic test traffic is flagged and must come out of a reported volume without being asked for.
cases.notes:
36 of the 1200 claims are is_test = true (3.00%), and the Health Insurance dataset carries a default-filter knowledge entry saying to exclude them from claims aggregates. March 2024 has 49 claims by service date and 35 once test traffic is dropped, so the two answers are far enough apart to be visible in a monthly volume report. Every claims reference in this suite obeys that entry; this is the case that makes it the question, so its wording must never pre-announce the filter — the agent has to apply it unprompted. The count is checked by the result set; the test|synthetic word check asks the answer to say it left test claims out. Guards against test claims leaking into reported volumes. Trap (validated 2026-09-23): the trapSql drops the default filter and returns 49 against the reference's 35.

Trap query (must return different rows): SELECT COUNT(*) AS claims FROM health_insurance.claims claim WHERE claim.service_date >= DATE '2024-03-01' AND claim.service_date < DATE '2024-04-01'

Paraphrases: How many claims had a service date in March 2024? | What was our claim count for services provided in March 2024?

cases.question: What have we paid out in each country?
cases.intent: Claims carry no country — the answer needs the member -> region -> state -> country hierarchy.
cases.notes:
The path is claims.member_id -> members.region_id -> regions.state_id -> states.country_code -> countries.name. Stopping one join short reports 8 regions or 6 states at the wrong grain; the correct answer is 2 rows, United States 58,862,147 cents over 1044 claims and Canada 6,510,043 over 120, the reference obeying the dataset's default filter and dropping test claims. The provider's location is not modelled at all, so country can only mean the member's. The totals are checked by the result set (the old text pattern on 58,862,147 would fail a correct "$588.6K"); the text check asks for the smaller country by name. Guards against answers that stop short of the requested grain and against inventing a country column on claims. Trap (validated 2026-09-23): the trapSql stops one join short, at the state, and returns 6 rows — Texas 21,616,213, California 20,291,583, New York 9,653,198, Ohio 7,301,153, British Columbia 3,543,149, Ontario 2,966,894 cents — against the reference's 2. Accepts cents or dollars — the question names no unit; alternative verified 2026-09-23: the same sum / 100.0 returns the same 2 rows, United States 588,621.47 and Canada 65,100.43 dollars, each exactly the reference ÷ 100.

Trap query (must return different rows): SELECT state.name AS state, SUM(claim.paid_amount_cents) AS paid_cents FROM health_insurance.claims claim JOIN health_insurance.members member ON member.id = claim.member_id JOIN health_insurance.regions region ON region.id = member.region_id JOIN health_insurance.states state ON state.id = region.state_id JOIN health_insurance.countries country ON country.code = state.country_code WHERE claim.is_test = false GROUP BY state.name

Alternative reference the branch also accepted: SELECT country.name AS country, SUM(claim.paid_amount_cents) / 100.0 AS paid_dollars FROM health_insurance.claims claim JOIN health_insurance.members member ON member.id = claim.member_id JOIN health_insurance.regions region ON region.id = member.region_id JOIN health_insurance.states state ON state.id = region.state_id JOIN health_insurance.countries country ON country.code = state.country_code WHERE claim.is_test = false GROUP BY country.name ORDER BY paid_dollars DESC, country.name

Paraphrases: How much have we paid per country? | Break down our total payments by country.

cases.question: What data do we have about denials?
cases.intent: Pure discovery — must answer from the session datasets rather than run SQL or invent entities.
cases.notes:
